idiom_name: non-virtual public skeleton + private virtual primitive operations (NVI)
implementation_notes: C++ members are non-virtual by default, so the skeleton needs no keyword and the varying steps are virtual: declare the entry point public and non-virtual, keep required steps private pure virtual (protected only when a sub-base legitimately calls them) and give hooks a default body. Sutter's Virtuality guidelines are the checklist - prefer non-virtual interfaces using Template Method, prefer private virtuals, promote to protected only for base calls, and give the base class a public virtual (or protected non-virtual) destructor - and `override` (C++11) turns a signature drift into a compile error. The naive public-virtual form of the pattern is justified only when subclasses are meant to replace the whole algorithm, which is exactly the case the pattern exists to prevent; when the concrete type is always known at compile time, the CRTP variant replaces the virtual hooks with static dispatch.
pitfalls: A derived class that declares an overload with the same name hides the base skeleton instead of overriding a step; mark overrides with `override` and keep hook names distinct from the entry point.
Never call a step from a constructor or destructor: during construction and destruction virtual dispatch stops at the class being built or torn down, so the override is silently skipped.
Private virtuals cannot be called by the derived class, so a hook that must extend its base implementation has to be protected - private is the default, protected the deliberate exception.
The destructor is the one operation the pattern cannot wrap: make it public and virtual when deletion through the base is allowed, or protected and non-virtual when it is not (Sutter guideline 4).

variants.name: CRTP: compile-time skeleton with static dispatch
variants.implementation_notes: The skeleton lives in a class template parameterised by the derived type and calls self().step(), so the compiler sees the concrete type and inlines every step with no vtable at all - the right form for embedded, hot or fixed-type code. cppreference's CRTP page shows the static_cast pattern (C++23 deducing-this removes the boilerplate), and the standard library uses it in std::enable_shared_from_this and std::ranges::view_interface. It replaces the virtual hook with monomorphised direct calls, but each instantiation is a distinct type: Pipeline<A> and Pipeline<B> cannot share a container, so keep the virtual form when the concrete type is only known at runtime.
variants.idiom_name: curiously recurring template pattern: Base<Derived>::run calling static_cast<Derived*>(this)->step()
pitfalls: CRTP instantiations are unrelated types: Pipeline<A> and Pipeline<B> cannot be stored in one container or passed through a common virtual interface without adding one.
Calling a step of the derived class from the base constructor runs before the derived object exists; keep the skeleton off constructors here as well.
Compile-time dispatch trades binary size and compile time for speed (one skeleton per instantiation), and a typo in a step name surfaces as a template error at the instantiation point.
